newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-DIAGANA'S GAMBLE BRINGS HIM WORLD GOLD MEDAL.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-DIAGANA'S GAMBLE BRINGS HIM WORLD GOLD MEDAL.

text.p: Frenchman Stephane Diagana compensated on Monday for the disappointment of missing last year's Atlanta Olympics by winning the world 400 metres hurdles title from the front.

Diagana, the European record holder and one of the most popular sportsmen in France, seemed destined to be remembered as an also-ran after finishing fourth in the 1992 Olympic final, fourth in the 1993 world championships and third in the worlds two years ago.
His medal hopes in Atlanta disappeared after he sustained a stress fracture in his foot and a knee injury this year appeared to end his hopes of a medal here.
He started training again in May and admitted he came into the championships having no idea how he would run.
But it all came right for him on Monday. His gamble to lead from the front paid off and he was never headed as he crossed the line in 47.70 seconds, the fastest time of the year.

South African Herbert Llewellyn, who turned 20 two weeks ago, added a world championship silver to the silver he won in the world juniors last year, while Bryan Bronson of the United States, had a poor race by his own high standards and had to be content with the bronze.
Llewellyn clocked 47.86 seconds, the third time this year he has run a personal and national record, while Bronson ran 47.88.
"I had no idea what my form would be here," said Diagana. "My performance in the first round was very poor, but it improved in the semifinal.

"I decided the only way I could win the race was if I went out hard, opened up as big a lead as possible and then try and hold on because I knew that Llewellyn and (Fabrizio) Mori would close on me at the finish and that is exactly what happened."
Diagana's first round time of 49.34 improved to 48.14 in the semifinal and finally 47.70, the fastest he has run since setting the European record of 47.37 in 1995.
While France was celebrating their first medal of the week, his coach Ferdinand Urtebise was ecstatic.
"This was Stephane's first major competition for a year and we left it to him to decide how to race.
"But he hasn't changed, he always likes the big challenge and he is not afraid of anybody. All he had to do was be prepared to take a risk and that's exactly what he did."
His father Lassana was another delighted onlooker.
"It really is a dream, but not a surprise," he said. "My wife Yvette and I knew it would happen it was just a question of when."
One close French athletics observer said Diagana's victory would be popular at home.

"The French people have a great affection for him," he said. "He is a throroughly nice guy who does a lot of work for charities and is head of the Groupement des Athletes Francais -- the French athlete's union. They will have a big party for him I am sure. After all the disappointments he has had, he thoroughly deserves it."
